## Psalm 149 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Background and Setting

This is one of the five final "Hallelujah Psalms" (Psalms 146–150), all of which begin and end with "Praise the LORD" (Hallelujah) and are entirely praise, containing no lament or complaint. The psalm has no title in the Hebrew text.

**Authorship and date:** Gill notes that Calvin and others thought it was written for Jews returning from the Babylonian captivity, while Theodoret saw it as predicting Maccabean victories. Gill himself leans toward Davidic authorship, referring to the Messiah. Ellicott thinks the Maccabean age is the most likely setting, noting the coincidence between v. 6 and 2 Maccabees 15:27, where the *chasîdîm* (the "godly ones" / "saints") fought with hymns in their throats and swords in their hands.
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/149.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-149.html

---

### v. 1: *"Hallelujah! Sing to the LORD a new song—His praise in the assembly of the godly."*

**"Hallelujah" / "Praise the LORD":** This one-word Hebrew exclamation frames the psalm at beginning and end. Spurgeon laments that the word Hallelujah is often used flippantly today and should be treated as sacred — "He who uses this word in a flippant manner is guilty of taking the name of the Lord in vain!"
- https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons43/sermons43.xi.html (Spurgeon exposition at end of sermon)

**"A new song":** Not necessarily a freshly composed tune. Spurgeon says, "He is ever new in his manifestations; his mercies are new every morning; his deliverances are new in every night of sorrow; let your gratitude and thanksgivings be new also." Guzik adds that an old saint can sing a new song when he gains fresh awareness of God's love. Gill identifies it as "the new song of redeeming grace through Jesus Christ, the song of the Lamb," distinct from the old song of Moses at the Red Sea — suited to Gospel times in which all things are made new.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/149.htm

**"In the assembly of the godly" (saints / *chasîdîm*):** Praise is wonderful when offered by the individual, but even richer in the gathered congregation. Ellicott notes that in the Maccabean period *chasîdîm* had become a regular title for the patriotic party of the faithful. Gill sees it as a picture of Gospel churches assembled for worship (citing Ephesians 5:19).
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-149.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/149.htm

---

### v. 2: *"Let Israel rejoice in their Maker; let the children of Zion rejoice in their King."*

**"Rejoice in their Maker":** Boice, cited by Guzik, notes, "The starting point for us creatures must be our acknowledgment of the Creator." Gill points out that the Hebrew can read "his Makers" (plural), suggesting the involvement of Father, Son, and Spirit in creation (as in Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man"), and in the formation of Israel as a people.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/149.htm

**"Their King":** God is Maker of all humanity but is recognized as King only over His people. Spurgeon says, "The true splendor of kings lies not in what their people do for them, but in what they do for their people: and herein our Lord excelleth all the princes that ever lived." Gill identifies this King as the Messiah, the King of Zion, whom the children of Zion — regenerate, church-member believers — should rejoice in.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/149.htm

---

### v. 3: *"Let them praise His name with dancing, and make music to Him with tambourine and harp."*

**"Dancing" or "pipe"?** There is a translation debate. The Hebrew *mahol* is rendered "dance" in most English translations, but Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik) and Ellicott argue it means a flute or pipe — a musical instrument. Ellicott says its use in Psalm 150 among orchestral instruments is "almost decisive" for "pipe," and the Syriac version translates it as a flute. However, Spurgeon takes it as dance but distinguishes it: "The holy dance of those days differed altogether from the frivolous and lascivious dances of the present time. It was a sacred exercise in which the whole body expressed its delight before God."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-149.html
- https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons43/sermons43.xi.html

**"Tambourine and harp":** Instruments of percussion and strings, used in ancient Israel's worship (Exodus 15:20). Gill notes these instruments were typical of the spiritual melody made in the heart, and that the instruments themselves "are now laid aside, being only suited to the church in her infant state." Matthew Henry adds a caution: those who use this verse to urge instrumental music in worship "must by the same rule introduce dancing," since both went together in OT practice; the NT canon for psalmody is to "sing with the spirit and with the understanding."
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/149.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/149.htm

---

### v. 4: *"For the LORD takes pleasure in His people; He adorns the afflicted with salvation."*

**"Takes pleasure in His people":** This is a breathtaking statement about God's disposition toward His people. Spurgeon asks, "What is there in us in which the Lord can take pleasure? Nothing, unless he has put it there. If he sees any beauty in us, it must be the reflection of his own face." Meyer adds, "It is the constant teaching of Scripture that we may please God." John Piper at Desiring God cites this verse as one of the "breathtaking statements from God's happiness in his people," alongside Zephaniah 3:17.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/preaching-the-gospel-of-the-happy-god
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps149.php

**"Adorns the afflicted / beautifies the meek with salvation":** The word translated "meek" or "afflicted" or "humble" can be rendered each way. Ellicott: "He adorns the oppressed with salvation" — the honour of victory is like a beautiful robe on the delivered people. Spurgeon reads three meanings: "He will beautify the meek with salvation," "He will beautify the afflicted with deliverance," and "He will beautify the meek with victory." He comments: "God taketh pleasure in all his children as Jacob loved all his sons; but the meek are his Josephs, and upon these he puts the coat of many colours." Maclaren: "The qualification for receiving Jehovah's help is meekness, and the effect of that help on the lowly soul is to deck it with strange loveliness." Matthew Henry: "When the Lord has made sinners feel their wants and unworthiness, he will adorn them with the graces of his Spirit."
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-149.html
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps149.php
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/149.htm

---

### v. 5: *"Let the saints exult in glory; let them shout for joy upon their beds."*

**"Exult in glory":** The saints rejoice in the glory God has put upon them (salvation, righteousness, grace) and in the glory they will have in eternity. Gill connects this to Romans 5:2 — rejoicing "in hope of the glory of God."
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/149.htm

**"Sing aloud upon their beds":** Waking hours do not provide enough time to praise God; praise continues even on their beds. Gill offers several layers: (1) meditating on God's word at night and giving thanks (Psalm 63:5); (2) praising upon waking after safe sleep (Psalm 4:8); (3) singing even on sickbeds, since God strengthens there (Psalm 41:3); (4) singing on one's deathbed the triumphant song, "O death, where is thy sting?" (1 Corinthians 15:55); (5) the grave itself is a bed where the flesh rests in hope. Matthew Henry similarly says, "Let them rejoice, even upon the bed of death, assured that they are going to eternal rest and glory." Ellicott suggests the "couches" might refer to divans at feasts rather than beds for sleep (cf. Hosea 7:14).
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/149.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/149.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-149.html

---

### v. 6: *"May the high praises of God be in their mouths, and a double-edged sword in their hands,"*

**"High praises of God" — literally, "exaltations of God" in their throat:** The Hebrew word for "mouth" here is actually "throat" (*gutture*), indicating deep, heartfelt praise, not mere lip service. Spurgeon: "God's people sing from their hearts and so they are a deep-throated people who do not merely sibilate praise with the lips, but send it up from the depths of their soul!" The phrase "high praises" (*romemot*) can also mean "the high things of God" — His perfections, attributes, and mighty works.
- https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons43/sermons43.xi.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-149.html

**"A double-edged sword in their hands":** The combination of praise in mouth and sword in hand is the psalm's most striking image. Spurgeon captures it memorably: "Songs in their mouths and swords in their hands! … God's people must sing and fight at the same time — and they fight best who sing best." He adds, "The word of God is all edge; whichever way we turn it, it strikes deadly blows at falsehood and wickedness. If we do not praise we shall grow sad in our conflict; and if we do not fight we shall become presumptuous in our song. The verse indicates a happy blending of the chorister and the crusader."

Under the New Covenant, the two-edged sword is identified with the Word of God (Hebrews 4:12, Ephesians 6:17, Revelation 19:15). Spurgeon is emphatic: "If you had a sword of steel, you would fight with men; but that is no part of your business. You are not called to that cruel work; but, as you have the sword of the Spirit…go forth and praise God by the use of that two-edged sword which is the Word of God."

G. Campbell Morgan: "Their praise is not merely to be that of the chanting of words. It is also to be in the doing of His will. While the high praises of God are in their mouth, a two-edged sword is to be in their hand, with which they carry out His purposes."

Guzik draws a parallel to the American WWII saying, "Praise the Lord and pass the ammunition," and applies it to church life: every gathering of God's people should excel in both praise and the preaching of God's Word.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/
- https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons43/sermons43.xi.html

---

### v. 7: *"to inflict vengeance on the nations and punishment on the peoples,"*

**The traditional reading:** Matthew Henry says some of God's servants of old "were appointed to execute vengeance according to his word. They did not do it from personal revenge or earthly politics, but in obedience to God's command." Gill sees a Gospel application: through the apostles' preaching, "vengeance" was taken on the pagan world as idolatry was overthrown, and particularly in the latter days against the antichristian system (citing Revelation 19:15). Poole, cited by Guzik, sees a literal historical fulfillment through David's victories over the Philistines, Ammonites, Syrians, and other neighboring enemies.

**The critical warning:** Maclaren: "The stern close of the psalm strikes a note which many ears feel to be discordant…. [Yet] it is entirely free from any sentiment of personal vengeance." Ellicott's introduction records Delitzsch's sobering observation: this psalm was misused by Caspar Scioppius to inflame Catholic princes to the Thirty Years' War, and by Thomas Münzer to stir up the Peasants' War. Morgan reminds readers, "There is no reference in this Psalm to the Church of God. As it specifically indicates, it has to do with 'Israel,' with 'the children of Zion.'"
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-149.html

**Spiritual application for the church:** Under the New Covenant, believers do not battle flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12-18). Guzik: "In a spiritual sense, we are to execute vengeance on every thing that would oppose Jesus Christ and the work of His kingdom in our lives." Matthew Henry likewise: "Let the high praises of God be in our mouths, while we wield the sword of the word of God, with the shield of faith, in warfare with the world, the flesh, and the devil."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/149.htm

---

### v. 8: *"to bind their kings with chains and their nobles with shackles of iron,"*

**Literal historical reading:** Matthew Henry sees this fulfilled by Joshua over the Canaanite kings, Gideon over the princes of Midian, and Samuel over Agag. Gill also notes David's victories over surrounding nations' kings and nobles.

**Spiritual reading:** Gill offers a Gospel-application: the two-edged sword of the Word binds Satan, the "strong man armed" who keeps the palace as a king, and dethrones sin which "reigns like a king unto death." Kidner, cited by Guzik, says: "Our equivalent of binding kings with chains (Psalm 149:8) is to 'take every thought captive to obey Christ' (2 Cor. 10:5)." Spurgeon applies it spiritually: "Oh, that God would help us to bind King Drunkenness with chains and King Infidelity with fetters of iron!"
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/149.htm
- https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons43/sermons43.xi.html

---

### v. 9: *"to execute the judgment written against them. This honor is for all His saints. Hallelujah!"*

**"The judgment written":** Several interpretations exist. Ellicott suggests it might be a specific written order from the military context, or refer to judgments registered in the sacred books against nations such as the Canaanites and Amalekites, or a more general sense as in Isaiah 65:6 ("Behold, it is written before me: I will not keep silence, but will recompense"). Gill sees it as the sentence written in the Law (Deuteronomy 7:12; 32:41) or in the Gospel (Mark 16:16 — whoever believes not shall be damned). For the believer under the New Covenant, Guzik says "there is a written judgment against every spiritual enemy, and Jesus wrote it by His work on the cross (John 16:11, Colossians 2:14)."

**"This honor have all His saints":** The honour is that of being instruments of God's righteous purposes — both worshipers and warriors in His cause. Maclaren: "They are redeemed from bondage that they may be God's warriors. The honour and obligation are universal." Matthew Henry: "The honour intended for all the saints of God, consists in their triumphs over the enemies of their salvation."
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-149.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/149.htm

**"Praise the LORD" / Hallelujah:** The psalm that began with Hallelujah ends with it, bringing the praise full circle.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/

---

### Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**The main point of divergence is how literally to read verses 6–9 (the warfare language):**

1. **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Takes Psalm 149 as "a particular psalm to Israel," with the warfare commands directly applying to OT Israel as the Mosaic covenant administrator. For the church, the two-edged sword is spiritual — the Word of God — and the vengeance language is applied to divine judgment at history's end.
   - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-149.html

2. **Reformed / Puritan (Spurgeon via Treasury of David):** Strongly spiritualises the sword as the Word of God. Insists believers have "no warrant of execution against our fellow men" and are "not called to that cruel work." Yet Spurgeon also applies it to spiritual warfare against specific societal evils (drunkenness, infidelity). Maclaren, also Reformed-leaning, says the NT equivalent is spiritual weapons — "the weapons of our warfare are not carnal" and there are "stronger fetters than those of iron, even the cords of love."
   - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/ (quoting Spurgeon and Maclaren)
   - https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons43/sermons43.xi.html

3. **Pentecostal / Charismatic (David Guzik / Enduring Word):** Emphasizes the inseparable link between praise and spiritual warfare — the "high praises of God" are themselves a weapon alongside the Word. Cites 2 Chronicles 20:20-21 where praise preceded victory. Warns strongly against any literal application of the violence language, noting the Thirty Years' War and Peasants' War as tragic misuses. Stresses that under the New Covenant, warfare is entirely spiritual (2 Corinthians 10:5; Ephesians 6:12-18).
   - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-149/

4. **Methodist / Wesleyan Holiness (Matthew Henry):** Though Henry predates modern denominational lines, his commentary is widely used across traditions including Methodist. He holds both a literal (for OT Israel) and spiritual (for the church) reading in tension. He insists, "Christ never intended his gospel should be spread by fire and sword, or his righteousness by the wrath of man." The saints' honour is their final triumph "through the blood of the Lamb and the word of his testimony." On instruments, Henry cautions that those who use this psalm to justify instrumental music in worship "must by the same rule introduce dancing," since both went together — the NT canon for praise is singing "with the spirit and with the understanding."
   - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/149.htm

5. **Lutheran:** No specific Lutheran commentary on Psalm 149 was found in the available searches from lcms.org or 1517.org.

6. **Reformed Baptist / New Calvinist (John Piper / Desiring God):** Piper focuses primarily on v. 4 ("the LORD takes pleasure in His people") as part of his theology of God's happiness. He does not extensively treat the warfare verses in the available material but cites this verse as evidence that God delights in His people.
   - https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/preaching-the-gospel-of-the-happy-god

7. **On musical instruments in worship (v. 3):** A secondary but notable difference emerges. Gill (a Baptist) says the instruments of the OT "are now laid aside, being only suited to the church in her infant state." Matthew Henry warns against using this verse as a proof-text for instruments without also accepting dancing. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes that Psalms 33 and 150 "specifically admonish and extol the use of mechanical, musical instruments," yet this is in the context of OT Israel.
   - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/149.htm
   - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/149.htm
   - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-149.html

---

### Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (bible.org / NET Bible notes):**

The Bible.org notes observe the grammatical structure: vv. 1–4 open with two parallel Piel imperatives followed by four imperfects used as jussives ("let Israel be glad," etc.). The psalmist "prays that Israel will respond appropriately to their military victory by recognizing it is from YHWH and not themselves." For v. 6, the "sword in their hand" is noted as possibly referring to: (1) literary imagery of a past victory, (2) a symbolic dance by priests, or (3) preparation for a coming battle. V. 7 is seen by some in an eschatological setting, though it could fit any historical victory. On v. 9, "the judgment written" must refer to "Holy War" promises as in the Exodus and Conquest.
- https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-149

**Catholic and Orthodox:** No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary was found through newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org in the available searches.

**Historical-critical view (Ellicott / Delitzsch):** The psalm most likely dates from the Maccabean age (2nd century BC), when the *chasîdîm* (Hasideans) fought literal battles against Seleucid oppressors while singing hymns. The "judgment written" may refer to specific military orders or to standing biblical judgments against pagan nations. Ellicott notes that the psalm has been tragically misused throughout history to justify religious violence.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-149.html

---

### Summary of Key Themes

Across all traditions consulted, several points are consistently emphasized:
- God takes genuine pleasure in His people — this is a stunning truth that fuels all praise (v. 4).
- Praise and spiritual warfare belong together; the Word of God is the believer's sword (v. 6).
- The violent language of vv. 7–9 must not be used to justify physical violence by Christians. It either describes OT Israel's unique calling, points to final eschatological judgment, or is applied spiritually to the believer's warfare against sin and spiritual enemies.
- The "honour" of being God's instruments — both in worship and in His work of setting things right — belongs to all believers (v. 9).
